en: The Scripture on Receiving the Ten Wholesome Precepts, translated during the Later Han Dynasty by an unknown author.
Chapter One: The Ten Evil Karmas. Chapter One: The Ten Evil Karmas.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada’s renowned wife, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra with a compassionate Brahma-voice:
"I shall now, for your sake, explain the removal of the retributions for the ten unwholesome evil deeds.
Listen attentively! Receive this with careful heed!"
Hold this in mind with single-mindedness; be careful not to forget it!
"The ten unwholesome karmas are:
first, the karma of killing;"
Second, the karma of stealing;
third, the karma of sexual misconduct;
fourth, the karma of false speech;
Fifth, the karma of divisive speech;
sixth, the karma of harsh speech;
seventh, the karma of frivolous speech;
8. The karma of covetousness;
9. The karma of malice;
10. The karma of delusion.

Śāriputra! You should now universally instruct all sentient beings to purify their physical actions, purify their verbal actions, and purify their mental actions; prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they should take refuge in the Upādhyāya and sincerely repent for these three evil karmas, reciting this three times.

Having already performed the confession, with body, speech, and mind purified, one should then successively announce one's own name and take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha;
this is to be recited three times.
Having completed the taking of refuge in the Buddha, having completed the taking of refuge in the Dharma, and having completed the taking of refuge in the Saṅgha;
thus it is said three times.
One should then further ask:
"O son of good family, O daughter of good family!
Are you able to uphold [this]?
If they say they are able to uphold it, one should further ask:
"Is there no fault or affliction in your body and mind now?

As for faults of the body, have you shed the blood of a Buddha, killed an Arhat, caused a schism in the Saṃgha, slandered and severed the roots of goodness, or acted in opposition to the Buddha’s True Dharma?"
If they say no, one should further ask:
"Do you harbor in your mind the intent to commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma?

Have you ever stolen property belonging to the Buddha, property belonging to the Dharma, property belonging to the noble Sangha, property belonging to the present Sangha, or property belonging to the universal Sangha?"
"Have you committed impure acts toward your mother, sisters, younger sisters, or bhikṣuṇīs?
If he says "No," one should further instruct him:

"Since your body and mind are now thus pure, O Virtuous One, please bear this in mind: I now wish to receive the precepts of the ten wholesome courses of action. I have already repented for my ten unwholesome courses of action; I only pray that the Virtuous One, out of compassion for me, will grant permission for me to uphold them!"
At that time, one should instruct them:

"Upāsaka [Name], Upāsikā [Name], you should now single-mindedly count the breaths, binding your mindfulness to the present, toward the seven Buddhas of the past, the Honored Buddha Śākyamuni of the present, and Maitreya and all other Buddhas of the future."
"Having instructed them to recollect the Buddha, one should say:

'May the Saṅgha of the seven Buddhas listen; may the Saṅgha of the Buddhas, including Śākyamuni, listen; may the Saṅgha of noble disciples—the Srotāpannas, Sakṛdāgāmins, Anāgāmins, and Arhats—listen. This layman [or] this laywoman, so-and-so, is pure in body, speech, and mind, and is fit to be a vessel for the Dharma.'"
"I now wish to request and receive the precepts of the ten wholesome mental states and the eightfold precepts.
Having thus made this request three times, he then instructs them, saying:
"I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Sangha."
Thus he says three times:
"Disciple [Name], I have completed my refuge in the Buddha; I have completed my refuge in the Dharma; I have completed my refuge in the Saṅgha.
Thus he says three times.

"O [Name], I call to mind that you shall firmly uphold this body: uphold the body as the Buddha, uphold the body as the Dharma, and uphold the body as the Sangha. Regarding the three karmas of the body—first, not killing; second, not stealing; and third, no sexual misconduct—you should receive and uphold these three bodily precepts for one day, ten days, or even for the rest of your life."
If they say they can maintain it, one should further ask:
"Do you now wish to perform a small portion of wholesome deeds,
or a great portion?"
"Are my wholesome qualities complete?
If he says, "I am able," one should further say to him:
"The facts are indeed thus; you shall follow the teacher's instructions."
"I, disciple [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
Thus one says three times.
"The taking of refuge in the Buddha is complete; the taking of refuge in the Dharma is complete; the taking of refuge in the Saṃgha is complete."
Thus he says three times:
"So-and-so, be mindful; guard your mouth, guarding the mouth as you would the Buddha, guarding the mouth as you would the Dharma, guarding the mouth as you would the Saṃgha."
The four actions of speech are:
first, refraining from false speech; second, refraining from divisive speech; third, refraining from harsh speech; and fourth, refraining from frivolous speech.
You should uphold these four aspects of speech for one day, ten days, or even for the rest of your life.
If they say they can uphold it, one should further ask:
"Do you now wish to perform a small portion of wholesome deeds,
or a great portion?"
"Is your virtue complete?
If he says, "I am able," one should further say to him:
"The facts are indeed as such; you shall follow the teacher's instruction."
"I, disciple [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha.
Thus it is said three times.
"The taking of refuge in the Buddha is completed; the taking of refuge in the Dharma is completed; the taking of refuge in the Sangha is completed."
Thus it was said three times:
"O [Name], be mindful; firmly uphold your mind. Uphold your mind as you would the Buddha, uphold your mind as you would the Dharma, and uphold your mind as you would the Saṅgha."
The three karmas of the mind are:
first, covetousness; second, malice; and third, delusion.
You should uphold these three mental karmas for one day, ten days, or even until the end of your life.
If they say they can uphold it, one should further ask:
"Do you now wish to perform a small portion of wholesome deeds,
or a great portion?"
"Are your wholesome qualities complete?
If he says, "I am able," one should further say:
"The facts are indeed as such; you shall follow the teacher's instructions."
If one receives the ten wholesome precepts but does not uphold the eight precepts, they will ultimately not be perfected;
if one violates the eight precepts, the ten wholesome precepts are extinguished together with them.

Disciple [Name], from this morning until tomorrow morning, may the Virtuous One bear me in mind; may the Virtuous One act as my Upādhyāya. Regarding the Dharma of the eight precepts, you should with a sincere heart firmly uphold these eight precepts.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, one maintains the mind as the Buddha;
taking refuge in the Dharma, one maintains the mind as the Dharma;
taking refuge in the Sangha, one maintains the mind as the Sangha.
Thus he says three times:
"I have completed my refuge in the Buddha; I have completed my refuge in the Dharma; I have completed my refuge in the Saṃgha.
Thus he says three times.

"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind: from this clear dawn until the next clear dawn, I wish to receive the eight precepts. I only pray that the Venerable sir, out of compassion, will grant me permission!
One should then further ask:
"Are you able to receive and maintain the eightfold fast?"
If he says he is able, [the preceptor] should say: "You must maintain your mind so that it is like that of the Buddhas and Arhats.
If he says he is able, one should further tell him:
"From the past limit until the present limit, during this interval, have you committed any offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (abandonment and confession) through body, speech, or mind?"

Such transgressions, even up to the most fundamental and gravest offenses, are now confessed with utmost sincerity before the Buddhas of the three periods, the Arhats, and the Sangha of preceptors, prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground to repent for all sins; this is called practicing the Dharma of Poṣadha.
Once the poṣadha has been performed, one is said to dwell in purity and is fit to be a vessel for the Dharma.
Next, you should receive and uphold the eight precepts of the Tathāgata.
Are you able to maintain them?
Thus he asked three times.
Regarding the eightfold precepts of the fast: these are the monastic rules established for laypeople by all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, of the past and present.
The first is: not to kill.
Second, not to steal;
third, not to engage in sexual misconduct;
fourth, not to speak falsely.
Fifth, not drinking alcohol;
sixth, not sitting on high or wide beds;
seventh, not going to witness or listen to performances by singers or musicians, and not wearing garments scented with perfumes.
Eighth, do not eat past midday.
You should uphold it in this way:
"Do not kill, nor steal; do not engage in sexual misconduct, nor speak falsehoods."
Avoiding alcohol and shunning the fragrance of flowers, refraining from high beds and eating after midday—
these are the things the Sages have all distanced themselves from;
you should receive and uphold these eight dharmas.

"By virtue of upholding this observance of the fast, one shall not fall into the hells, nor into the realm of hungry ghosts, nor into the animal realm, nor into the asura realm; one shall always be born among humans, leave the household life with right view, and attain the path to nirvana."

If they are born in the heavens, they will always be reborn in the Brahma heavens; they will encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world, request him to turn the wheel of Dharma, and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to praise this Dharma, spoke in verse:
"If one can practice the ten wholesome deeds And accord with the teachings of the True Dharma,
One shall see the Buddha in every birth, And both body and mind will be fully liberated."
Forever freed from all bonds of suffering, may you swiftly attain the unsurpassed path.
If a person observes the eight precepts, following the Vinaya and conforming to the Prātimokṣa,
upholding the True Dharma of all Buddhas without violation—
"You should know that body and mind are simultaneously liberated.
This is called the path to nirvana, the practice of all Buddhas.
Having spoken this verse, he addressed Śāriputra:

"You should properly uphold the ten wholesome paths of action and the eight precepts; be careful not to forget or lose them, lest you destroy the seeds of the Dharma. Expound them extensively for all devas and humans."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, so it is; we shall respectfully receive and uphold it!
At that time, Śāriputra and those in the assembly who had heard what the Buddha taught rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter Two: The Rewards of the Ten Acts of Giving From the *Sutra on Receiving the Precepts of the Ten Wholesome Actions* The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"All who take birth cherish their own bodies and lives;
therefore, one should practice giving, extending universal compassion equally toward all sentient beings."
To regard all beings as one’s own eyes—this is called the precept against killing.
This has been taught by all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, the Omniscient Ones:
"Use yourself as a metaphor; do not kill, and do not wield the rod."
If one sees a being being killed, it is as if a blade were piercing one's own heart.

Viewing all sentient beings as no different from oneself, one maintains this precept of non-killing to be reborn in the heavens and to constantly encounter the assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; such is the reason for upholding the precept of non-killing.
Because he bestowed fearlessness upon all, at the end of his life he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
where he enjoyed himself with elephants, horses, and jade maidens. In the Brahmā Heaven,
within palaces of maṇi and vaidūrya, colored like white silver and golden flowers, he constantly sat upon a sublime seat made of the seven treasures.

Golden mechanisms and precious vessels, flowers of the seven jewels, and immeasurable celestial maidens performing music, they bear his feet and lift the palace as it travels through the void; wearing jeweled crowns upon their heads, they sit in the central hall.
Abandoning lust and entering meditative absorption, they encounter the Buddhas who proclaim the Four Truths;

awakening to them, they swiftly attain the stage of Srotāpanna. Some leap for joy and resolve upon the Great Mind, destined to achieve the path to Bodhi in the future; others are reborn in Tuṣita or Yama.
The Śuddhāvāsa devas, the Ābhāsvara, the Brahmakāyika, the Puṇyaprasava, the Ābhāsvara, and the Śubhakṛtsna,
up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven— these,
together with the Bodhisattvas of Great Compassion, sit, lie, move, and rest, sharing the same food and drink.
Constantly listening to the Dharma throughout the six periods of day and night, Maitreya Deva King shall always preach for him;
he will practice the non-retrogressive turning of the Great Dharma Wheel.
In the future, he shall surely behold Maitreya, who will subdue Māra, attain Buddhahood, and turn the Dharma Wheel; there, within that Buddha’s Dharma, he shall go forth as a monk.
Furthermore, one beholds the thousand Tathāgatas of the Bhadrakalpa; Vairocana Buddha bestows upon them the prophecy of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called the most supreme fruit of non-killing, and it is also called the root of the Brahma-faring of compassion.
That which has been taught by all Buddhas, that which has been practiced by all Buddhas:
"Love for one's eyes and ears, love for one's children is likewise;
love for one's own life is boundless; therefore, do not kill."
This is called the supreme holy life (*brahmacarya*).
One should not eat meat; seeing a killer is like seeing a thief, for one must know that such a person will surely fall into hell.
Those who eat meat fall frequently ill; by taking life, they merely adorn themselves.
One should practice a heart of great compassion and uphold the precept against killing; thus, one will surely attain the path to Bodhi.
He addressed Śāriputra:
"You should now know that the karma of taking life is extremely grave!
In the past, when I was traveling with you through the city of Pāṭaliputra, there was the daughter of an elder in that great city named Devavatī."
She gave birth to a son, peerless in his handsome features, like a red lotus flower, incomparable even to celestial maidens.
His mother cherished him deeply; she carried him to my presence and addressed me, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"My son is lovely, like a celestial youth.
My love for this child exceeds my love for my own body by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
At that time, I said to him:
“Good daughter, you should know!
All ordinary beings cherish their own lives, like the ocean swallowing rivers, never reaching satiety.
How can you now say that you love your son? What proof do you have for this?”
Then the woman said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
I love this child so dearly that even if a fire were to break out and consume my body, I would never let him go."

At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to transform her, employed his supernormal powers to manifest four yakṣas. Each carried a mountain of fire, approaching from the four directions. When the fires were still at a distance, the woman used her own body and her garments to shield the child. As the fires drew closer, she raised her hands to cover her face and held the child out to block the flames.
The Buddha said to the good woman, "You say you love your son; how can you hold your son as an obstruction to the fire while seeking to save yourself? Then that woman replied:
“World-Honored One!
We pray only that you save us; we do not begrudge this child.
The Buddha withdrew his supernatural power, and mother and son were cooled and refreshed; they immediately gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.
The Buddha told the woman:
"You cherish yourself and you cherish your son.
Why then would you take your own life or incite another to kill?"

One should know that taking life brings about a great and evil retribution; one will certainly fall into the most intense place of suffering, the Avīci Hell, and be subject to the jurisdiction of King Yama.
What is called the most severe law and code?
King Yama, during the six periods of day and night, proclaims that the retribution for killing involves ten evil karmas:

"First, the karma of killing leads to constant rebirth in the Hell of the Blazing Blade-Mountain, where one is sliced and cut by blades and wheels, dismembered limb by limb until reduced to eighty-four thousand pieces."
In a single day and night, there are sixty billion births and sixty billion deaths.
At that time, King Yama rebukes the offenders:
"You delighted in taking life; now you undergo this suffering."
Is this matter pleasant?
You shall now have to repay the debts you owe others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, and even then they will never be exhausted!

"Second, those who commit the karma of killing will certainly be reborn in the Sword Forest Hell (*asipattravana*). There are eighty-four thousand sword-trees, each eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height. Each tree produces eighty-four thousand sword-branches; each branch produces eighty-four thousand sword-flowers; and each flower produces eighty-four thousand sword-fruits. This person who killed beings climbs upon the sword-trees, their mind reaching the tops of all the sword-trees, while their remaining limbs and joints are covered throughout the sword forest. Each joint reaches eighty-four thousand sword-branches, which shave the bones and penetrate to the marrow. The sword-flowers and sword-fruits leave no part untouched; the body is shattered and destroyed like a mustard seed."
In a single day and night, there are eighty-four thousand births and eighty-four thousand deaths; such is the nature of the karma of killing.
Then King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in killing, and now you undergo this suffering."
"Is this matter pleasant?
You shall now, for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, repay the debts you owe others, and even then it will never be exhausted!

'Thirdly, the karma of killing leads to rebirth in the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons. After hundreds of thousands of millions of boils, the flesh is consumed until only bone remains; one is placed upon a copper pillar and spontaneously returns to life. Hundreds of thousands of thorns transform into iron blades with which one cuts off one's own flesh to eat, only to fall back into the cauldron."
In a single day and night, there are eighty-four thousand births and eighty-four thousand deaths.
At that time, King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in killing living beings; now you undergo this suffering."
"Is this matter pleasant?
You shall now have to repay your debts to others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, and even then they will never be exhausted!

"The fourth is that the karma of killing leads to birth in the Iron Bed Hell. There is an iron bed there, exactly fifty yojanas in length and breadth; iron spikes from all four directions come together to pierce the heart, while a great iron-meshed chariot rolls over the crown of the head and emerges through the feet."
In a single day and night, there are eighty-four thousand births and eighty-four thousand deaths; such is the nature of the karma of killing.
Then King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"Because you delighted in killing, you now undergo this suffering."
"Is this matter pleasant?
Furthermore, you shall now have to repay the debts of others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, and even then they will never be exhausted!

"Fifth, the karma of killing leads to birth in the Iron Mountain Hell; the iron mountains on the four sides are shaped like iron caves, and from within these caves, fire erupts from all four directions."
There are five yakṣas who hack the bodies of the offenders into four pieces and cast them into the fire; then the four mountains close together, crushing and scattering them like dust.
A fire-bird suddenly arises, and iron-beaked crows as well as iron snakes enter through his joints, breaking his bones and extracting his marrow.
In a single day and night, he undergoes eighty-four thousand births and eighty-four thousand deaths; such is the nature of the karma of taking life.
Then King Yama rebuked the sinner:
"You delighted in taking life, and now you undergo this suffering.
Is this matter pleasant to you?"
"Now you must further repay the debts you owe others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, yet they will never come to an end!

"Sixth, the karmic retribution for killing leads to birth in the Iron Net Hell. There is a great iron mountain a hundred thousand yojanas high, filled with molten iron. Above it is an iron net; through each opening of the net, countless and boundless iron-beaked insects enter from the crown of one's head, piercing the bones and penetrating the marrow, then splitting out through the feet."
In a single day and night, there are eighty-four thousand births and eighty-four thousand deaths; such is the nature of the karma of killing.
At that time, King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in killing, and now you undergo this suffering."
"Is this matter pleasant? You shall now have to repay your debts to others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, and even then they will never be exhausted!

"Seventh: The karma of killing leads to rebirth in the Crimson Lotus Hell. There is a lotus flower with eighty-four thousand petals; each petal is shaped like a mountain of blades, five yojanas high. Ten billion forests of swords are simultaneously ablaze. When the sinner sits within, one petal of the flower opens. As each petal opens, the volcanic mountains and sword-forests burn the flesh and shatter the bones, causing a hundredfold agony. When these features close together, hundreds of thousands of mountains of blades slice into the body at once."
In a single day and night, there are eighty-four thousand births and eighty-four thousand deaths; such is the nature of the karma of killing.
Then King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in killing, and now you undergo this suffering."
"Is this matter pleasant? You shall now have to repay your debts to others for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, and even then they will never be exhausted!

"Eighth: The karma of killing leads to rebirth within the Five Deaths and Five Lives Hell. There are five great mountains there; atop each mountain are fifty billion razor-wheels, and above these razor-wheels are great wheels of water. Within them, the offenders' bodies bloom like flowers as they lie upon cold ice. From the five directions, the five mountains and razor-wheels come toward them, crying out, 'Live! Live! They are then split into five pieces; through five deaths and five lives, their bodies are crushed into dust."
In a single day and night, there are eighty-four thousand births and eighty-four thousand deaths; such is the nature of the karma of killing.
Then King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in killing, and now you undergo this suffering."
"Is this matter pleasant?
You shall now have to repay your debts to others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, and even then they will never be exhausted!
(9) Ninth, through the karma of killing, one is born within the Forest of Venomous Snakes hell."

There are immeasurable poisonous serpents of glowing iron, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; each serpent is several thousand yojanas long and spews poison from its mouth like glowing iron balls. This poison enters through the crown of the sinner’s head and permeates every single limb and joint throughout his body;
there are also immeasurable snakes that vomit poison and fire, incinerating the sinner.
In a single day and night, there are eighty-four thousand births and eighty-four thousand deaths; such is the nature of the karma of killing.
Then King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in killing, and now you undergo this suffering."
"Is this matter pleasant?
You shall now have to repay the debts you owe others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, and even then they will never be exhausted!

"Tenth: The karma of killing leads to birth within the Iron Shackles and Collars Hell. There, iron mountains twelve *yojanas* high serve as shackles; iron pillars sixty *yojanas* tall with nets of fire serve as chains; iron dogs eighty *yojanas* long spit fire from their mouths as cangues; and iron arrows from the void fall of their own accord to pierce the heart. From these cangues, shackles, and collars, copper balls are transformed and produced, entering through the eyes and spreading across all the limbs and joints before exiting through the feet."
In a single day and night, there are eighty-four thousand births and eighty-four thousand deaths; such is the nature of the karma of killing.
Then King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in killing, and now you undergo this suffering."
"Is this matter pleasant?
You shall now have to repay the debts you owe others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, and even then they will never be exhausted!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"The karma of killing results in suffering within the hells; this is called the 'flower-retribution' (the preliminary fruit).
Subsequently, when one is born among humans, one suffers from many illnesses and has a short lifespan.
Furthermore, being born among the various sentient beings of the four modes of birth, one undergoes manifold sufferings that are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable."
“What is called the precept against stealing?

The precept against stealing consists in universally bestowing wealth and external life upon all sentient beings; for this reason, the Buddhas have taught that the precept against stealing is called ambrosia, coolness, and peace. To uphold this precept is called the path to heaven, the place of attaining the Way, the robe of nirvana, and the life of liberation.”
Therefore, all Buddhas praise non-stealing as it severs the cause for becoming a hungry ghost.
There are ten kinds of evil that are the retribution for stealing:

First, the retribution for stealing is that one will certainly fall into the Flesh Mountain Hell (*māṃsaparvata-naraka*). In this hell, the sinners have necks as large as great mountains and possess hundreds of thousands of heads. On the cheeks of each head, fleshy protuberances grow, from which hundreds of thousands of iron dogs emerge from the iron mountains, snarling and howling as they scramble to devour them.

There are iron nails that emerge from the mouths of dogs, enter through the crowns of the offenders' heads, and exit through their heels. Their skin is flayed and spread upon iron spikes extending for hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*. Both body and skin endure suffering for eighty-four thousand years; the pain is like being cut with knives, a torment difficult to bear. This is called the first retribution for stealing.
At that time, King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in stealing; now you undergo this suffering.
Do you find this pleasant?"

"You must now, for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, repay the debts you owe others; it shall never come to an end! "Second, as retribution for stealing, one is born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

One's body is extremely large, fifty *yojana* in height; the sound of one's walking is like that of five hundred chariots; fire blazes from the joints of the limbs like ten burning chariots; one starves while devouring iron balls and thirsts while drinking molten copper; one's hair is like iron thorns, entangling the body. For hundreds of thousands of millions of years, one undergoes immeasurable suffering, never hearing the sound of water or grain. This is called the second fruit of retribution for stealing."
Then King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in stealing and now undergo this suffering.
Do you find this pleasant?"
"You must now, for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, repay the debts you owe others; even then, they will never be exhausted!

Third, as retribution for stealing, one is born within the Cold Ice Hell. For hundreds of thousands of millions of years, mountains of ice from the eight directions serve as clothing, spreading out like blooming lotuses; one eats one's own flesh while flaming arrows pierce the heart. This is the third karmic fruit of theft."
Then King Yama rebuked the sinner:
"You delighted in theft and now undergo this suffering.
Is this matter pleasant to you?"
"Furthermore, you shall now have to repay the debts of others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, yet they will never be exhausted!

"Fourth, as a retribution for stealing, one is born among the rākṣasas. The females are like celestial maidens with handsome features; the males have a thousand eyes, their heads are bound with iron chains, and dog-like fangs protrude upward. Fire erupts from the tips of their ears. When the females assume seductive poses, their entire bodies burst into flames. They drink blood and eat flesh; they eat fire and eat charcoal; they consume pus and vomit. For hundreds of thousands of millions of years they endure the bodies of rākṣasas, experiencing extreme suffering and distress. This is the fourth karmic fruit of stealing."
Then King Yama rebuked the sinner:
"You delighted in theft and now undergo this suffering.
Is this matter pleasant to you?"
"You shall now, moreover, repay the debts you owe others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, yet they can never be exhausted!

"Fifth is the Iron Deer Hell, the retribution for theft: one takes the form of an iron deer with hundreds of thousands of heads, hundreds of thousands of hands, hundreds of thousands of tails, hundreds of thousands of hooves, and hundreds of thousands of layers of skin."

Five hundred billion iron tigers and hundreds of billions of iron lions flay their skins; from between each skin grow immeasurable iron thorns like swords and blades, which cut through the bones and penetrate the marrow. The suffering is immeasurable, and for hundreds of thousands of millions of years they undergo endless torment. This is called the fifth retribution for stealing.
Then King Yama rebuked the sinner:
"You delighted in stealing and now undergo this suffering.
Do you find this pleasant?"
"You shall now, for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, repay the debts you owe others, and even then they will never be exhausted!

"Sixth, as a retribution for stealing, one is born among humans, naked, black and emaciated, with eyes that roll askance and breath that is foul and stinking. One constantly dwells in prison, is employed to clear away filth, and serves as a messenger for the royal household. Though born among humans, one's appearance is like that of an ox or a horse; the father does not love the son, nor is the son filial to the father; the mother does not love the son, nor is the son filial to the mother. For hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, the suffering is immeasurable. This is called the sixth retribution for theft."
Then King Yama rebukes the sinner:
"You delighted in stealing and now undergo this suffering.
Do you find this pleasant?"
"You must now, for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, repay the debts you owe others;

it shall never come to an end! "Seventh, as retribution for theft, one is born in the Great Hell of Sword-Flowers. There are immeasurable and boundless forests of knives and swords. The bodies of the sinners are like iron cauldrons, equal in length and breadth to hundreds of thousands of yojanas. The hell-wardens drive and kick them like wind blowing flowers, causing them to be born upon the tips of sword-flowers. Hundreds of thousands of sword-flowers flay their skin into countless pieces, carving through their bones to the marrow, and they fall from the sky.

When they are born upon knife-flowers, the thorns of the knife-flowers flay their skin into immeasurable pieces, splitting their bones into countless fragments, piercing the marrow and stabbing the heart; though they seek death, they cannot find it."

From the iron mountains on the four sides, immeasurable iron caltrops are produced through transformation; like arrows from a great crossbow, they simultaneously pierce the heart. For immeasurable billions of years, one undergoes such suffering—this is the seventh retribution for stealing.
Then King Yama rebuked the sinner:
"You delighted in theft and now undergo this suffering.
Is this matter pleasant?"

"You must now, for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, repay the debts you owe others; it shall never come to an end! "Eighth, as retribution for stealing, one is born in the Great Hell of the Volcanic Earth.

One assumes the form of a great prisoner with hundreds of thousands of heads, upon whose back one carries five hundred fire-bodied monkeys. Holding flaming knives in their hands, they flay the skin and cast it onto the volcanic mountains. Fire-wolves arise from within the heart, gnawing at the bones and penetrating the marrow. The body becomes a mass of fire as one flees in all four directions; passing through the volcanoes, one can never escape. Enduring myriad forms of suffering, one seeks death but cannot find it, undergoing such torment for hundreds of thousands of millions of years."
Then King Yama rebuked the sinner:
"You delighted in theft and now undergo this suffering.
Do you find this pleasant?"
"You shall now, for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, repay the debts you owe others;

they can never be exhausted! "Ninth, as retribution for theft, one is born in the Great Earth Hell of Pierced Noses. In this hell of pierced noses, there are twelve iron hooks that hook the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and tongue; clubs are used to break the teeth, and the skin of the face is flayed and transformed into pieces of flesh which are placed inside the mouth. It becomes a great flaming arrow that shoots from the heart down to the feet; though one seeks death, it cannot be found, and such suffering is endured for hundreds of thousands of millions of years."
Then King Yama rebuked the sinner:
"You delighted in stealing and now undergo this suffering.
Do you find this pleasant? You must now repay your debts to others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; it shall never come to an end!"

"Tenth, as retribution for stealing, one is born into the Hell of Butchery and Flaying. Lying upon an iron table, the hell-wardens use knives to flay the skin and cut out the heart; yet one refuses to die, suffering in this manner for hundreds of thousands of myriads of years."
Then King Yama rebuked the sinner:
"You delighted in theft and now undergo this suffering.
Is this matter pleasant to you?"
"You must now repay the debts you owe others for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, and even then they will never be exhausted!
What is called the precept against sexual misconduct?
The precept against sexual misconduct possesses five meritorious benefits, which have been praised by all Buddhas of the past, present, and future.
As for being free from lust, one abides in the majestic deportment of a Buddha and possesses a bodily fragrance like that of a Buddha.

What are the five [qualities]? First, one does not stir the eye-consciousness and does not gaze upon lustful forms. Even when seeing forms, it is as if seeing dung-worms; it is as if a blade were piercing the heart, or as if fire were burning the eyes. The mind does not give rise to craving. Cut by impermanence, the fires of the eyes move recklessly—how could there be any love?

"Second, one does not hear lewd sounds; even if one hears lewd sounds, the ear-consciousness remains unmoved and the faculty of hearing is not gratified by them. Foolish sounds agitate the forest of poisonous snakes and serve as seeds for craving; these are called 'thieves' winds' that emerge from the faculty of hearing, arising from false perceptions like the chanting of yakṣas—what craving could there be in such things!

This is an illusory echo; fools cherish it, causing their sense faculties to be stirred. This is but the voice of a person in the dew, flowing along the current of the five desires from the river of delusion and craving. Knowing this well to be a thief, one remains unmoved by the ear-consciousness.

"Third, when the faculty of the nose smells an odor, one should know that this odor arises from the eight winds: stirred by the wind of ignorance and blown hither by the wind of craving, various fragrances such as those of flowers are produced from false imagination and exist erroneously. Arising from the nose-consciousness, one falsely claims it is a fragrance or praises it as a delicious scent; the nose-consciousness is thus agitated, and all grasses, trees, and myriad flowers are likewise called fragrant. The Tathāgata restrains his body and does not smell scents or stenches; understanding in his essence that they are not real, he does not praise their fragrant touch."

"Fourth, they do not move the tongue-consciousness; they do not speak of worldly gain, nor do they praise sexual matters. Their mouths never speak of the touch-pleasures of lust, nor do they dwell in the delusive, sticky houses of infatuation. Furthermore, they do not delight in speaking of things that increase ignorance, the five thieves, and the delusion of craving. For this reason, the Buddhas do not move their tongue-consciousness."

"Fifth, the mind is tranquil and unmoving; it does not give rise to lustful thoughts, does not dwell upon lustful matters, does not conceive of lustful pleasures, and does not stir the root of lust. Lustful consciousness does not turn; like a liberated mind, it dwells in the state of cessation, abides in the city of eternal bliss, and rests in peace and non-action. Following and learning from the Buddha-mind, it dwells at the limit of True Suchness (Tathatā), entering single-mindedly into the eighteen great emptinesses and the nine kinds of nirvana."

“Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain five merits: their physical forms are pure and they are always born from lotus flowers; their bodies are stainless and their minds are serene. For this reason, the Buddhas proclaim the precept against sexual misconduct as the most supreme purity and unsurpassed merit, endowed with five benefits, praised and extolled as the cause of liberation, inexhaustible.”
Sexual desire is an extremely heavy bond that cannot be untied; it is like an old elephant mired in the mud of the five desires, serving as the universal root of all transgressions.
I shall now speak of the sin of lustful desire:
"Listen with a single mind: sexual impurity is an evil that obstructs the ten thousand practices."
Sinking into various meditative absorptions obstructs the path to liberation.
Sons and daughters of good family who seek the path to liberation and wish to leave behind the prison of the triple world—
the fire-pit of the five desires and the river of sensual craving— must do so.
Like escaping from boiling water, fire, cold, or ice, one should liberate oneself from the fear of birth and death;
holding the mind as the Buddhas do, one should uphold the precept against sexual misconduct.
If you seek long life in the heavens, with a lifespan of immeasurable kalpas, [you must uphold this precept].
Brahmā and the Wheel-Turning King possess the seven treasures of wealth;
holding their minds like those of the Buddhas, they should maintain the precept of celibacy.
Those who wish to behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and realize the fruits of the Path, [should likewise maintain this precept].
Possessing the six supernormal powers, Wandering through the lands of the ten directions,
Maintaining the mind as the Buddhas do— One should uphold the precept against sexual misconduct.
There are ten faults and afflictions of sexual misconduct.
What are the ten?

"First, those who are greedy and lustful, though they may be born in the heavens as Śakra, Lord of Devas, and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, their minds are like dogs stealing food; they are perpetually intoxicated and do not awaken, submerged in the swift-flowing river of the five desires."

"Second, those who are greedy and lustful, though they may be kings of men with sovereign power and authority, become slaves to their own passions and are driven like wild men; even if they acquire great wealth and treasures, like fire consuming fuel, they know no satiety, resulting in the ruin of themselves and their nations, and upon death, they fall into the evil realms."

"Third, those who are greedy and lustful are constantly bound to others; driven by the six thieves, they are trampled upon the back by the great elephant of impermanence. Their minds are like monkeys, ignorant of manifold hardships; burned by the fire of desire, they fail to recognize their parents, brothers, or sisters. Like pigs and dogs, they carry one another's burdens, devoid of all shame or remorse."

"Fourth, those who are greedy for lust constantly drink the impure pus and blood of women; throughout immeasurable kalpas they always dwell within the womb, where the stomach, the large intestine, and the uterus serve as their dwelling, and various worms serve as their clothing. They gnaw upon the female organ, using it as their food and drink."
"Fifth, those who are lustful have minds like sharp blades and eyes like flaming chariots; they cut away and incinerate the treasury of their meritorious conduct.
Sixth, when lustful people enter an assembly of Kṣatriyas, they kindle the fire of the fetters and pile on the fuel of craving, desiring to plunder them just like rākṣasas;
when they enter an assembly of Brāhmaṇas, they feel no shame or remorse, acting like illusory beings who perform sorcery and speak only of impure matters."

Having arrived among the assembly of śramaṇas, they do not know how to take refuge; their sensory faculties stir like glue adhering to grass. They are surrounded by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of desire that defile them, and the fire of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) blazes up, burning the seeds of goodness. They destroy the pure karma and holy conduct (*brahmacarya*) of previous lives; their every movement of hand or foot is like a sharp blade, their eyes are like fierce fires, and their mouths are like rākṣasas. Every pore of their entire bodies is driven by the fire of lust.

"Seventh, those who are greedy and lustful commit eight kinds of karma: killing; creating instruments for killing such as swords, blades, and staves; bringing men and women together; committing great falsehoods; drinking alcohol; singing songs that create the conditions for lust; or further, stealing all manner of precious vessels and ornaments from insect-infested places. Driven by the King of the Mind, their sense-faculty of the eye—like a vicious dog—steals and devours what is foul and filthy."

"Eighth, those who are greedy for lust are driven by their passions; their minds are like a great fire or a mass of heated iron. They will surely fall and sink, destroying their pure conduct (brahmacarya), and will inevitably fall into hell."
"Ninth, those who are greedy and lustful, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life—like the brief moment it takes to toss a shell or a pearl—will certainly fall into the Red Copper Hell."

The Tāmra-dhūma Hell is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth, equal in all dimensions. It is like a grove of copper flowers; beneath it lies an iron bed, and upon the bed stand hundreds of thousands of yojanas of hot copper pillars with eight facets. At the tops of these pillars are mirrors, within which naturally appear images of women or men. The lustful person becomes attached to them, and as their sensory faculties are stirred, fire breaks out simultaneously. The copper flowers transform into large, scorching iron nails, and the copper pillars turn into boiling molten copper. The cauldrons, the iron beds, and the fires blaze forth; the women become dogs and the men become knives. They drive and kick the offenders, who undergo immeasurable suffering: they chew hot iron balls and swallow molten copper. Though they seek death, they cannot find it, passing through immeasurable years with a lifespan of one kalpa.

"Tenth, those who are greedy and lustful shall not behold the Buddha, for like being obstructed by heavy clouds, they have destroyed their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). They will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell, where their bodies will fill the entire prison for the duration of one kalpa; rolling back and forth within it, they shall further pass another kalpa."
Then King Yama rebuked the sinner:
"You delighted in lustful desires and now undergo this suffering.
Is this matter pleasant?"
"You must now, for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, repay the debts you owe others; they can never be exhausted.

When his life in hell ends, he will be reborn among pigeons and doves, and take the form of dragons and snakes. Because he defiled the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), for hundreds and thousands of lifetimes he shall not see a Buddha nor hear the Dharma, and in the end, he shall not attain the Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Sensual desire is not severed; it continues on, giving birth to sentient beings.”
With ignorance as the root, one is cut by the blade of old age and death.
One needlessly encounters a forest of venomous snakes;
this blood-filled bag of impurity is like a dung-worm delighting in filth—so too it is with those who crave lust.
The nine orifices flow with the fire of desire; affection and love are like poisonous thorns.
Perverted and false views arise, and through delusion, craving is born.
All female forms are slippery, like trees blooming with wild flowers.
Blown by the winds of perversion, the withered flowers swarm with insects.
A woman is like a painted jar, from which drops of pus and blood flow;
though the jar is full, it leaks and overflows, its impurities filling the space without.
Seeing impure fluids with one's own eyes, like a thieving dog coveting lewdness, one should extinguish all cravings within oneself. With a single mind, contemplate the impure;
drink the nectar of immortality and dwell in the city of Great Nirvana.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“If there are those who guard their minds and bodies so as not to commit sexual misconduct; who guard their eyes so as not to look at lustful forms; who guard their ears so as not to listen to lustful sounds; who guard their noses so as not to smell lustful fragrances; and who guard their tongues so as not to taste lustful flavors—such persons are said to be fully endowed with wisdom and to walk the Eightfold Noble Path.”

Purity of body and mind through celibacy is like a lotus flower, which is unstained by dust and grime; the attainment of the path of the Srotāpanna, the path of the Sakṛdāgāmin, the path of the Anāgāmin, the path of the Arhat, the path of the Pratyekabuddha, and the unsurpassed Great Way—all are obtained through the purity of celibacy.
Regarding the four karmas of speech: false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, and speech that praises wrong views:
"If one can refrain from false speech, One preaches the precept against lying;
Maintaining the mouth as the mouth of a Buddha, One always speaks words of truth."
Such a person is born in the heavens, their fragrant breath perfuming all the celestial realms;
if born in the human world, they are adorned with every kind of fragrance,
like the waters of the Fragrant Mountain flowing into the river of Nirvāṇa.
If one can refrain from double-tongued speech, the mind will likewise be free of duality;
the tongue will become like the tongues of all Buddhas, with lotus petals covering the face,
emitting five kinds of variegated light from its features.
Always speak the Dharma of the great person; with utmost sincerity, refrain from double-tongued speech.
If one can also avoid harsh words, such a person is called a great man (mahāpuruṣa), upright among men, whom all delight to behold.
Like the blended fragrance of sandalwood, if one can refrain from frivolous speech,
the mouth will constantly emit a wondrous scent, like that of the utpala lotus.
Born into a place where one meets a Buddha, the karma of speech is purified according to reality.
If one does not praise wrong views, nor speaks of the karma of wrong views;
if one is always born as a renunciant and is constantly endowed with right livelihood;
if one dwells in nirvana just like the Buddha—all these are obtained through truthful speech.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Regarding the four verbal transgressions, there are ten great evil karmas. What are these ten?"

"First, there is the person who speaks falsely and slanders others: one who claims to have heard what was not heard, who claims to have attained the fruits of the Path when they have not, and who claims to have seen what was not seen. Such an evil person, though not afflicted by physical illness, is like a leprous dog."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Among all gods and humans, even a fierce fire burning iron balls that burns and destroys all people— this thief is not superior to them."
What constitutes a great thief?
It would be better to have one's joints set ablaze, one's bones transformed into molten copper,
to swallow and devour upon a mountain of knives, or to be dismembered by boiling cauldrons, blades, and saws.
One’s body is shattered and turned into a mass of fire; this suffering does not arise from evil deeds.
False speech is a great poison that burns away the merit of devas and humans, causing one to wander through the Avīci Hell with wheels of swords for feet.
With an iron venomous snake for a tongue, its mouth-fire burns the great trichiliocosm;
its eyes are like flying iron pellets, raining down showers of boiling cauldron-soup.
It scorches and destroys the flowers of one’s roots of goodness, ensuring one's certain fall into the evil realms.
For immeasurable billions of kalpas, there is no way to escape from seeking [liberation].
Such a person of great evil has their entire body as a mountain of fire,
burning away all that is wholesome.

"As for those who engage in harsh speech, though their mouths may contain fragrant incense, they smell like a corpse; they constantly delight in speaking of others' various unwholesome deeds, and what they utter from their mouths is like thorns, like knives, like swords, like halberds, like excrement, like urine, like insects, and like pus."
"Among the fragrances of gods and humans, nothing surpasses wholesome speech;
among the stenches within the three realms, nothing surpasses harsh speech.

Second, when a person of harsh speech utters words from their mouth, they are like raining down iron balls that incinerate and destroy the homes of others; such a person will fall in the future into the great hell, where hot iron burns their body and they drink molten iron."

If they are born into the world, they become diseased, leper-like dogs or diseased, leper-like humans; for immeasurable kalpas, they constantly consume pus and blood, and whatever their minds conceive is purely unwholesome and associated with evil.

"Third is double-tongued speech. A person who engages in double-tongued speech is like water and fire; they claim to do what they have not done, and when others perform good deeds or speak pure and truthful words, they recklessly and perversely declare them to be wrong. They falsely attribute to others actions that those people did not commit. All people in the world constantly take no pleasure in seeing such a person. They will certainly fall into the great evil realms, where their tongues will be sawn with copper saws into thousands of pieces."

"Fourth is frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). Frivolous speech consists of inverting what is high to make it low, and inverting what is low to make it high; it is playful and unrestrained, employing clever words and sharp rhetoric. It involves speaking useless words, speaking unbeneficial words, and speaking meaningless words; it includes praising the five desires, speaking with an unclear mind, and speaking dark words. Like thorns and like forests, it ensnares sentient beings."

When this person’s life ends as a retribution for their evil deeds, they shall fall into the Forest of Thorns Hell (*Kaṇṭakavana-naraka*). There, hundreds of thousands of iron thorns will hook their tongue and tear it into hundreds of thousands of pieces.

Fifth, they praise wrong views. A person of wrong views has a mouth like a blazing fire that burns away all roots of goodness. They deny the existence of father and mother; they deny the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; they deny the Arhats, the Pratyekabuddhas, teachers, friends, and spiritual mentors (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The mind is like a swift wind that blows down all trees of the roots of goodness; this is a great thief.

Proclaiming that there is no cause or effect, its mouth is like a vast torrent that flows recklessly through the three realms. Indulging in lust without restraint, it mocks and deceives its own kind. It commits the five deeds of immediate retribution, severs *prajñā*, violates the four grave prohibitions, and reaches the level of the sins of the Avīci hell—all arising from wrong views and an inverted, evil mind.
When the evil winds of unwholesome and non-virtuous speech blow, the fires of the Avīci hell and iron thorns will grow upon one's tongue.
Know that such a person—whether they speak falsely, with harsh words, with double-tongued speech, or with frivolous chatter, or whether they praise false views—is a great evildoer;
though they remain in this world, composed of the four elements and adorned with the five aggregates, they should be understood as such.
The earth element consists of iron mountains, forests of swords, and trees of blades with hundreds of thousands of iron thorns;
there are countless iron insects, iron-beaked birds, iron nets, and barbed wheels that crush and sever their bodies.
One should know that water and fire consist of molten copper, countless cauldrons of boiling broth, and hot iron balls. Iron...
The river flows through the intervals between the joints; one should know that these large and small joints are naturally so.
It is like a bronze pillar from which many fires simultaneously arise from the six sense bases, burning and destroying body and mind, causing one to fall into the great hells.
One should know that the wind element is like hail and rain, and that countless forests of blades and hundreds of thousands of sword-trees shake the limbs.
The joints grow from the valleys; you should know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are themselves the five thieves.
The eighteen *rākṣasas* belong to the lineage of the prison and are subjects of King Yama. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is like glowing iron, appearing like molten copper, filling the Avīci Hell.
Self-exalting, arrogant, and robust, possessing great strength and foul speech, they revile, slander, and disparage others.
"Where is such a person now? The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"One who uses harsh speech, speaks falsely, engages in double-tongued speech, utters frivolous talk, and praises wrong views—such a person does not act as a thief against a single individual, but acts as a great bandit against all the devas and the people of the world."
Suppose there were a band of thieves possessing great power and authority who burned down a city and slaughtered all its inhabitants, as well as all the people throughout the four continents.
How great would the retribution for the sins committed by these individuals be?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The offense committed by this person is as vast as Mount Sumeru and cannot be measured.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Although this person shall receive the retribution for a great sin, it is not as grave as the great and heavy retribution obtained from the momentary commission of false speech, harsh words, double-tongued speech, frivolous talk, or the praising of wrong views. At the dissolution of the body after death, such a person falls into the great hells, where they undergo inexhaustible suffering for immeasurable kalpas, and even hundreds of thousands of Buddhas would be unable to save them."

The Buddhas observe that these people who slander the Dharma are born together with those in the hells of the worlds of the ten directions and perish together with them; therefore, the wise should restrain their body and speech!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If there are those who receive and uphold these ten precepts of good conduct and destroy the ten unwholesome karmas, they will be reborn above in the heavens as Brahmā Kings, or reborn below in the world as Universal Monarchs (Cakravartin Kings), teaching through the ten virtues and forever parting from the hells and the three evil paths; it is like flowing water reaching the ocean of Nirvāṇa.
If there are those who violate the ten precepts of good conduct, they will fall into the great hells and undergo various sufferings for immeasurable lifetimes."
“Śāriputra! You should well receive and uphold the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) for the ten wholesome precepts, and destroy the ten unwholesome karmas.
At that time, Śāriputra and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching on Receiving the Ten Wholesome Precepts.
